chapters.title: Why here — the meaning of tartuk

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So let's fast-forward to now. A lot of you know about this event happening in October, which is 5,000 people, or you just learned about it tonight. And part of what I realized I was doing — obviously, I was following what my teachers told me to do, first of all. But I went back and started analyzing: what did they tell me to do? And that's why I want to talk about it here at Casa Tartuk. For 500 pesos. Why are we doing this at Casa Tartuk? Because of the anniversary, but there's a more specific reason.

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Teachers? For the teachers that giving classes?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: No. Yes.

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: The people here in Casa Tartuk are your Mexican friends, and they're the ones that helped you change.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: That's true, but not the $500 answer.

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: You're sharing your own limiting beliefs so we can shift ours as well, and spread more to the Americas.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Muy buen dicho, pero no. Everyone put your hand out for a second. If your answer is more than one word, it's wrong. The name of this center is Casa Tartuk. What does tartuk mean?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Rejoice. Be happy.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Rejoice. It has a very, very specific meaning. And this is what my teachers taught me. And that's what Geshe Michael has been teaching as well, for those of you who've been studying with him over the last year or so.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So I have two hypotheses, two ideas I'm going to share tonight. One is about tartuk — tartuquear. It's about what it means to really rejoice in your goodness. And I'm going to propose that one of the reasons we haven't reached the goals we want to reach is because we're just not thinking about the goodness that we're already doing. And even if we are doing it, we're not doing it with good technique.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And then secondly, which is a corollary to the first one — I actually will propose that I don't think we have to do much more and struggle with goodness. We have to focus more on what we just need to remove and stop. We spend so much time, too much time, thinking about our faults and our weaknesses. All the things that have gone wrong in life. All the choices we made that went right instead of left. We mourn them, we grieve them. And they become part of who we are, as our identity.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Can someone give me a pen, please?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Here's my mic-drop moment. If you don't hear anything else, this is the thing to remember tonight.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The script that is running, that defines the person that you are, allows certain seeds to ripen and certain other seeds not to ripen. And if you don't change that, you can be the best seed-planter ever in the world, and those seeds just won't ripen.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: That was a philosophical point of view. Let's understand it with a dog. Who here has not heard the thing about the pen and a chew toy? Good. {laughs} Because I don’t want to explain it. But if there’s one person here, we would have done it. Is there anyone online who didn’t hear it? {no signs of new people} Okay.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So, we’re going to go deeper into the pen, but we have to do just a little bit of the pen story—not the whole thing—to understand what I’ve just said.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: For you as humans, if you are who you look like you are — ¿Qué es? {showing a pen}

paragraphs.speaker: Interpreter
paragraphs.text: What is this?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: This is a pen. For you, no problem. Méi wèntí (没问题, no problem) in Chinese. And I’m saying Chinese on purpose, for a reason. In Chinese it's a bǐ (笔, pen). But it doesn't matter what you call it — a pen, a pluma, el bolígrafo, bǐ — the words don't matter. But for humans, this is a pen, right? No one's going to disagree with that.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: My little puppy comes in the room, and I shake this object. What does the dog do? {put a pen in their mouth} They try to chew on it. For the dog, is this a pen? No. It's a chew toy. It can't be a pen. It could never be a pen for the dog.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Okay, so here's my point. Get your brains on. For the dog, a seed opens in their mind for a chew toy. Does a dog have a seed for a pen to open? Well, careful with the language. Does a seed for a pen open in the dog's mind? No. Okay, we can agree to that, right?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Does a dog have a seed for a pen? Maybe. Possibly. And we're not going to go into the Classics course four to prove past and future lives right now. Don't worry about that right now. But let's pretend that a dog has a seed for a pen in their mind-stream — it's just hanging out there. Can it ripen as a dog? No. But the seed's still there, right? Okay. So what’s happened with that seed? {laughs}

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So the question is: for a dog, it's impossible for a pen to ripen, correct? Even if it has a seed from a past life for a pen. Don’t worry about what I just said it’s part of the argument.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Now let's go to humans. In the mind of a human, you look at this object and it goes, pooh — pen, right? Is it possible for a seed of a chew toy to ripen in your mind?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience (Alex Rivas)
paragraphs.text: No, you’re chewing a pen.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: You can chew on it, of course. You can use it as a weapon. But it’s a pen that is being used in a specific manner.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The airlines worry about the wrong objects. They should worry about a pen. Don't worry about my four ounces of toothpaste. So just stick with me. Can a seed for a chew toy, the way that a dog sees a chew toy, open up in your mind? But do you have seeds for chew toys in your mind-stream? Quite possibly, right?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So what is it that makes that seed ripen for a pen in the human identity, that doesn't allow for a pen in the dog identity to arise?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Another seed.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: She's close. But look — there is a collection of seeds ripening for you right now that says, that is your mind and body. And there's a flow of that. It's like a cascade of you, you, you, mind and body, just flowing. And you just call that “Sophie” or “Tim” or “Gina” or “Aldo”—whatever your name is. That's just flowing. Think of it as the set of seeds that are just ripening as you. In you, what's possible? Pens are possible.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Now, if you're a dog, you have a flow of seeds of mind and body that go woof, woof, woof. You wag your tail. In that collection of seeds, the conditions, the identity that are available only allow for chew toys to arrive. Is everyone with me so far?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: All right. This wasn’t the class. It was, but it’s not. I still didn’t start the Power Point yet. I just made a Power Point so people could have good seeds.
